item.title: Defence Brief: Trump Orders US-South Korea Drills Scaled Back as Seoul Refuses Iran War Role; Raytheon Lands $22.9B Tomahawk Deal
item.description:
Washington's decision to cut the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises over Seoul's refusal to join the Iran war marks a major shift in the US-ROK alliance posture, while the Pentagon locks in a seven-year Tomahawk production surge and Japan's arms market opens to Europe's Helsing.
► US-South Korea Alliance Posture Shifts as Trump Cuts Joint Drills President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to 'substantially reduce' the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea, which began Monday as scheduled, citing Seoul's refusal to take part in the US war against Iran and his 'very good relat Why it matters: This is the first time in over 70 years a US president has unilaterally curtailed the core US-ROK deterrence exercise, and it signals that alliance commitments are now conditional on participation in Washington's conflicts. It also hands North Korea a diplomatic win and raises questions about extended deterrence credibility across Asia.
► Raytheon Locks In $22.9B Tomahawk Deal to Lift Output Past 1,000 a Year The US military awarded Raytheon, an RTX unit, a $22. 9 billion seven-year contract to expand Tomahawk cruise missile production, completing a preliminary framework agreement reached in February, Reuters and The Independent report. Why it matters: The 16-fold production increase reflects how badly the Iran conflict depleted US cruise missile inventories, and the multi-year contracting model signals a structural shift toward long-horizon industrial base commitments rather than annual stopgap buys.
► Japan's Arms Market Opens: Helsing Enlists Rakuten to Sell Strike Drones to GSDF German defense-AI firm Helsing has enlisted Japanese e-commerce and finance giant Rakuten to broker the sale of its unmanned systems to Japan's Ground Self-Defence Forces, Reuters and The Next Web report. Why it matters: A consumer-tech conglomerate acting as a weapons broker is a measure of how far the defense boom has spread beyond traditional primes, and it signals Japan's reformed procurement system is now actively courting foreign autonomous-weapons suppliers as it races to close a drone gap.

Why it matters: The lease underscores India's urgency in closing a maritime surveillance gap in the Indian Ocean as it waits for its purchased fleet, and reflects the broader pattern of India using US platforms to accelerate capability while building toward indigenous production.
► L3Harris Ousts CEO Kubasik Over Conduct Breach, Names Insider Mehta L3Harris Technologies said Chairman and CEO Christopher Kubasik left the company after a board investigation found he engaged in conduct inconsistent with the defense contractor's code of conduct, sending shares down 3. 3%, Reuters reports. Why it matters: The abrupt leadership change at a top-tier US defense contractor comes amid a period of heavy Pentagon demand and a delayed missile-unit spin-off, adding governance uncertainty to a company central to US munitions and space programs.

item.title: Defence Brief: Pentagon Locks In Seven-Year SM-3 Supply Deals With Boeing and RTX as Interceptor Replenishment Drags On
item.description:
The Pentagon signed seven-year framework agreements with Boeing and RTX to expand production of Standard Missile-3 components, part of a broader push to put the defense industrial base on a wartime footing after the Iran war drained interceptor stockpiles. Separately, Lockheed and Raytheon are stalling on the promised Patriot license for Ukraine, and CENTCOM stood up a multinational attack-drone task force.
► Pentagon Locks In SM-3 Supply With Boeing and RTX The Pentagon signed two seven-year framework agreements with Boeing and RTX on Friday to expand production of critical components for the Standard Missile-3, the Navy's primary ship-launched ballistic missile interceptor, Defense News reports. Why it matters: The Pentagon is shifting from buying finished interceptors to locking in subcontractor capacity years ahead, a recognition that the Iran war exposed how thin the missile supply chain really is. The SM-3 line is now a strategic bottleneck, not just a procurement line.
► Patriot License for Ukraine Stalls as US Giants Hedge Though President Donald Trump promised Kyiv a license to build Patriot interceptors at the July NATO summit in Ankara, Lockheed Martin and Raytheon have put the brakes on a joint-production deal, Defense News reports. Why it matters: The gap between Trump's political promise and what the two US primes will actually do reveals the core tension of the moment: Washington wants Ukraine armed, but the incumbents who dominate antiballistic missile production have little incentive to create a cheaper competitor that could undercut their monopoly.
► CENTCOM Stands Up Multinational Attack-Drone Task Force U. S. Central Command announced it will stand up Task Force Falcon Strike, its first task force focused on multi-domain, multinational attack drones, Defense News reports. Why it matters: CENTCOM is institutionalizing the one-way attack drone as a core warfighting tool and, crucially, folding regional partners into it. This is a shift from buying drones to building a multinational drone-operating architecture in the Middle East.

Why it matters: The program is a direct response to the Iran war, where U. S. air defenses intercepted Iranian missiles but the Pentagon grew concerned its own missiles are vulnerable to peer air defenses. The emphasis on affordability and non-traditional contractors signals a push to make hypersonics a mass-producible weapon, not a boutique one.

A cheap, reusable seeker directly attacks that constraint and could reshape how many guided weapons the US can buy and sustain.

item.description:

Separately, Ukraine's Fire Point is now producing about 100 long-range cruise missiles a month, and Portugal signed a home-grown drone deal.

► Portugal Buys Home-Grown Tekever AR5 Drones for Maritime Patrol Portugal's Air Force has signed a contract with Portuguese firm Tekever to supply AR5 drones for maritime surveillance, with delivery due in early September, Euronews and European Pravda report. Why it matters: The deal is a small but telling example of European states buying home-grown unmanned systems validated in Ukraine combat, and of the AR5's dual civilian-military utility — a pattern likely to grow as NATO members seek maritime domain awareness without relying on US platforms.

► NATO Air Defense and Russian Power Centers Under Drone Pressure Two ongoing developments illustrate the reach of drone warfare. Why it matters: These are incremental but telling: NATO's eastern flank is now routinely intercepting Russian drones over allied territory, while Russia's own symbolic naval display is being curtailed by the same unmanned-strike threat Ukraine is industrializing.
